title: How to Handle Your Husband: 10 Respectful Ways to Connect
h1: How to Handle Your Husband: 10 Respectful Ways to Work Through Anything Together
description: Wondering how to handle your husband when things feel tense? Try 10 respectful, practical ways to communicate, resolve conflict and feel like a team again.
excerpt: “Handling” a husband works best when it means partnering with him. Here are 10 respectful ways to talk, resolve conflict and reconnect.
intro:
Every marriage has stretches where you look at your husband and think, “How do I even deal with this?” Maybe he shuts down during arguments, forgets what you asked, works too much or seems distant. It is tempting to search for tricks to manage him. But the approaches that actually work are not about control; they are about creating conditions where two adults can hear each other.

This guide reframes “handling” your husband as handling your marriage together. You will get 10 practical, respectful strategies for talking, resolving conflict and reconnecting, plus guidance on when it is time to bring in outside help.
body:
What “handling” your husband should really mean

If “handling” means getting him to do what you want through pressure, guilt or games, the results tend to be short-lived and resentment builds on both sides. If it means understanding him better, communicating clearly and solving problems as a team, it can transform a marriage. Every strategy below assumes you are equals who both deserve respect, and that he is expected to put in the same effort.

Communicate in ways he can actually hear

1. Value his perspective, even when you disagree

Many people feel more cooperative when they feel their opinion matters. Ask for his input on decisions big and small, and listen to his reasoning before you respond. You do not have to agree. But “I hear why that matters to you” goes a long way toward lowering defenses, and it models the same respect you want from him.

2. Choose a good time to talk

Timing is half the conversation. Raising something serious when he walks in the door, while he is driving or late at night when you are both exhausted rarely goes well. Try “Can we talk about the budget after dinner?” rather than launching in cold. Giving a heads-up also helps partners who need a little time to process before discussing feelings.

Tip: Start hard conversations softly. Something like “I feel overwhelmed with the evening routine and I'd love your help figuring it out” gets a better response than “You never help.” Describing your feeling and a specific need invites teamwork instead of defense.

Build goodwill every day

3. Make him feel loved and appreciated

When life gets busy, appreciation is often the first thing to go. Notice what he does well and say it out loud: thanking him for handling the car, telling him he is a great dad, sending a text in the middle of the day. Couples researcher John Gottman describes “bids for connection,” small attempts to get a partner's attention or affection. Turning toward those bids, rather than ignoring them, builds the goodwill that carries you through harder moments.

4. Follow through on his requests, and expect the same

Reliability builds trust. If he asks you to pick something up or remember an appointment, doing it shows you take him seriously. The same goes for him. If one of you keeps forgetting, try a shared calendar or a running list on the fridge, so it becomes a system problem rather than a character flaw.

5. Protect quality time together

Kids, jobs and screens can turn spouses into roommates. Schedule time that is just for you two: a weekly walk, a standing date night, coffee on the porch before the house wakes up. It does not have to be expensive. The goal is regular moments where you talk about something other than logistics. For ideas, see our guide on how to grow your relationship.

Handle conflict as a team

6. Fight fair instead of avoiding every argument

Conflict is normal; how you handle it matters. Healthy couples still disagree, but they do it without contempt, name-calling or stonewalling. A few ground rules:

  • Stick to one issue at a time; avoid bringing up every past grievance.
  • Use “I” statements: “I felt hurt when…” instead of “You always…”
  • Take a 20-minute break if either of you gets flooded, then come back.
  • Look for a compromise rather than a winner.

7. Stay open-minded about his way of doing things

He may load the dishwasher differently, parent with a different style or relax in ways that baffle you. Ask yourself whether something is truly a problem or just a different preference. Letting go of the small stuff frees up energy for the issues that really matter, and makes it easier for him to stay open to your ideas, too.

8. Support his goals and share yours

Strong marriages make room for both partners to grow. Ask about his ambitions, whether that is a career change, a fitness goal or a creative project, and look for ways to cheer him on. Then share your own goals and ask for the same support. A marriage where both people feel encouraged to become their best selves tends to feel more like a partnership and less like a negotiation.

9. Apologize, and forgive, sincerely

Everyone gets it wrong sometimes. A real apology names what you did, acknowledges the impact and says what you will do differently, without “but.” When he apologizes sincerely, let it land rather than holding the mistake over him. Forgiveness does not mean pretending something did not happen; it means not letting it run the relationship. Repeated patterns, however, deserve a deeper conversation rather than endless forgiving.

Get outside help sooner rather than later

10. Consider marriage counseling early

Many couples wait until things are dire before seeing a counselor. Going earlier, when communication is strained but goodwill still exists, often makes the work easier. A licensed couples therapist can help you break cycles you keep repeating, like one person pursuing and the other withdrawing. If he will not go, you can still go on your own to get support and clarity.

Common situations and what to try

  • He shuts down during arguments. Many people withdraw when they feel overwhelmed. Agree on a short break and a specific time to return to the topic, so the pause does not become avoidance.
  • He works all the time. Talk about what you miss rather than what he does wrong: “I miss our evenings together. Can we protect two nights a week?”
  • The mental load is uneven. List household tasks together, including the invisible ones like scheduling appointments, and divide ownership, not just help.
  • You disagree about money. Hold a monthly money date with a clear agenda. Discuss values first (security, freedom, generosity), then numbers.
  • You feel like roommates. Bring back small rituals of connection: a six-second kiss hello, a walk after dinner, a question at bedtime about his day.

In each case, you are not trying to fix him. You are inviting him into solving a shared problem, and staying open to his ideas about what you could do differently, too.

When it's not a communication problem

These strategies assume a basically safe relationship between two people who both want it to work. Some situations call for different steps:

  • You feel afraid of his reactions or walk on eggshells to avoid anger.
  • He controls money, your phone or who you see.
  • He belittles, threatens or physically hurts you.

No amount of “handling” fixes abuse, and it is never your fault. Our guide on how to deal with a narcissistic husband covers more on manipulative dynamics, and how to leave your husband can help you plan if you decide to go.

Tip: If you feel unsafe at home, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is free, confidential and available 24/7 at 1-800-799-7233, by texting START to 88788 or at thehotline.org.

The bottom line

The healthiest way to “handle” a husband is to stop handling and start partnering: talk at the right time, start gently, appreciate each other, fight fair and get help early when you are stuck. Most importantly, these efforts should go both ways. If you want ideas for your side of the partnership, read how to be a better wife, and if things feel serious, our guide on how to save a relationship offers next steps.
takeaways: Treat “handling” your husband as partnering with him, not controlling him.
Pick good timing and start hard conversations gently with “I” statements.
Appreciation, quality time and fair fighting build goodwill that lasts.
Counseling works best early; abuse is never a communication problem to manage.

faq.q: How do I deal with a husband who doesn't listen?
faq.a: Choose a calm time, keep the request specific and short, and explain why it matters to you. Ask him to repeat back what he heard to check understanding. If not listening is a pattern, talk about it directly, and consider couples counseling to work on communication habits together.

faq.q: How can I make my husband understand my feelings?
faq.a: Describe the feeling and the specific situation rather than criticizing his character, for example “I felt lonely when we didn't talk all weekend.” Ask for one concrete change. Then invite his perspective. People understand feelings better when they do not feel attacked.

faq.q: How do I handle an angry husband?
faq.a: If he is angry but safe, give space to cool down and revisit the issue later with clear ground rules. If his anger includes threats, intimidation, breaking things or hurting you, that is not something to manage. Reach out to the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 for confidential support.

faq.q: When should a married couple go to counseling?
faq.a: Consider counseling when the same arguments keep repeating, you feel more like roommates than partners, trust has been damaged or one of you is thinking about leaving. Earlier is better, because counseling is easier while goodwill still exists. You can also attend on your own.
